summary: Angels take human wives and have giant offspring while violence spreads among living creatures. God judges the angels and their children, preserves Noah, and sends the flood; the chapter then tracks the ark and the recession of the waters until Noah releases its passengers.
whyItMatters: The flood is presented as judgment on pervasive corruption, while Noah's rescue gives the narrative a surviving line for the post-flood world.

context.author: Within the book, the angel of the presence dictates the account to Moses; the historical writer is unnamed.
context.audience: Israel is addressed through Moses in the book’s frame; the specific first historical audience is not identified.
context.date: The narrative places the revelation at Sinai; the historical Hebrew work is usually dated to the second century BCE, without an established exact year.
context.setting: The world before and during the flood, with dates marking construction of the ark, inundation, and drying land.
context.literaryForm: Judgment narrative joined to a dated flood chronology.

before.text: The preceding genealogy has introduced Noah and described Enoch’s testimony against the Watchers.

here.text: The chapter brings that corruption to judgment while preserving Noah through the flood and the ark.

after.text: After the ark opens, Noah offers sacrifice and receives instructions and a covenant sign for the post-flood world.

outline.heading: Angels, giants, and spreading violence
outline.note: The world’s corruption is contrasted with Noah finding grace.

outline.heading: Judgment on the angels and universal accountability
outline.note: The text describes binding, destruction, and recorded judgments.

outline.heading: Noah and the ark
outline.note: Noah is preserved and enters the prepared vessel.

outline.heading: Floodwaters rise
outline.note: Waters come from above and below before the ark rests.

outline.heading: The waters recede and the ark opens
outline.note: Dated stages lead to dry land and the release of living creatures.

keyVerses.text: But Noah found grace before the eyes of the Lord.
keyVerses.why: Noah's grace is the decisive contrast after the description of pervasive corruption.

keyVerses.text: And He commanded Noah to make him an ark, that he might save himself from the waters of the flood.
keyVerses.why: The command to build an ark begins the concrete means by which Noah is saved.

questions.question: How does this chapter connect the Watchers to the flood?
questions.answer: It opens with angels taking human wives and giant offspring, then describes widespread lawlessness. The narrator places judgment on those angels and their children beside the judgment of the violent world.

questions.question: What are the giants in this story?
questions.answer: The text calls the sons of the angels and human women giants, then says their line is destroyed. It gives no measurements or detailed biography of them here; their place in the chapter is tied to the outbreak of violence and judgment.

questions.question: Why are the angels bound while their sons are killed?
questions.answer: The chapter assigns different judgments to the fathers and their offspring: binding for the angels and the sword for their sons. It does not explain why the sentences differ, so that distinction should be reported rather than turned into a hidden system.

questions.question: What does the chapter say about fair judgment?
questions.answer: It says judgments are written for every creature and that God does not accept bribes or favor the great over the small. This moral statement sits inside the flood account and helps explain why the destruction is framed as judgment rather than accident.

questions.question: Do verses about a new righteous nature mean all beings have already stopped sinning?
questions.answer: The statement occurs in a sweeping description of God’s judgment and intended righteous order. The chapter itself continues with Noah’s rescue from a corrupt world, so a reader should not make it a claim that every later person is already sinless.

questions.question: Why is Noah spared when others are not?
questions.answer: The narrator says Noah found grace, describes his heart and conduct as righteous, and says his acceptance also preserved his sons. The chapter does not imply that the floodwaters were harmless to everyone outside the ark.

questions.question: What are the flood-gates and the fountains of the deep?
questions.answer: They are the chapter’s paired images for water pouring from the heavens and rising from below. Their sevenfold description belongs to this ancient flood narrative, not to a modern hydrological account.

questions.question: When does the ark open in this telling?
questions.answer: The narrative dates the entry, the rising and retreat of the waters, dry earth, and finally the opening of the ark. Noah releases the animals only after the text says the land is dry.

glossary.def: The offspring of angels and human women in this chapter’s primeval account.
An image for openings in heaven through which the floodwaters descend.
